2. The crates the check buys change over time. In frame 1 the check buys 10 crates, and the last one is dark. By frame 4 the last crate is greyer. In frames 5 and 6, at age 85, the check buys about 9 of the original 10 crates. The check itself shrinks and the crate row shifts, which suggests rising prices are eating into what it buys. The "+2% a year" label shows the check rising, but not by enough to fully keep up.

3. It means that a payment that rises 2% a year only partly keeps pace with consumer prices. Over about 20 years, Ruth's purchasing power falls to roughly 90% of her first check's. A flat payment would fall further, though the animation doesn't show that case.

4. A viewer might take away that purchasing power erodes over a long retirement, even with a payout that rises 2% a year. They might weigh a payout option with annual increases against a level one when comparing annuity quotes. That is my reading of the context. The frames give no explicit recommendation. They also say "history, not a forecast" and "ILLUSTRATIVE", so the numbers shouldn't be treated as a prediction.

5. The animation itself doesn't state any advice. The idea that inflation erodes income is what it shows. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion, drawn from the annuity-quote context in your prompt.
